claims.text: The baseline eutectic high-entropy alloy has a lamellar dual-phase microstructure.
The baseline alloy exhibits a strength–ductility trade-off.
Approximately 0.5 at% Boron will be added during alloy synthesis.
Minor Boron addition will induce coherent nanoscale precipitates at eutectic interfaces.
The interfacial nanoprecipitates form because Boron segregates to eutectic interfaces.
The proposed nanoprecipitates act as dislocation barriers and thereby increase strength.
Boron-induced precipitates refine the interface structure and distribute strain more homogeneously.
The modified interface activates additional plasticity mechanisms.
The proposed interface modification improves ductility.
Boron doping will simultaneously increase yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation to failure relative to the undoped baseline.
The predicted improvement applies under room-temperature tensile testing at standard structural strain rates when heat treatment is held constant.
The effect may not persist at extreme temperatures or under markedly different processing conditions because segregation behavior and precipitate stability can change.
The optimum Boron concentration for coherent nanoprecipitate formation is not known.
Processing parameters may influence precipitate morphology, distribution, and stability.
Undoped and approximately 0.5 at% Boron-doped samples can be compared while holding casting and annealing parameters constant.
TEM and atom-probe tomography can test whether coherent interfacial nanoprecipitates formed.

The hypothesis is falsified if the Boron-doped samples lack simultaneous statistically significant improvements in strength and ductility or if the predicted coherent nanoprecipitates are absent or incoherent.
